summary: Describes methods of carrying Key Performance Indicators using the Network Service Header (NSH), for example to monitor latency and QoS marking to find problems on some links or service functions. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Writing timing notes right on each packet as it passes through service stops, so you can spot where it gets slow.

questions: measure latency in service function chaining
how do you monitor service function chains
subtitle: Monitoring latency and quality of service in service function chains.

tldr.problem: Service providers deploying network services across multiple virtual and physical functions cannot easily see where latency and quality of service problems occur in the chain.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8592 describes methods of carrying Key Performance Indicators in NSH metadata, allowing each service function in the chain to stamp packets with latency and QoS information as they pass through, and a final node to export the data for analysis.
tldr.outcome: Service providers gain visibility into the performance and configuration of service function chains, enabling diagnosis of problems without out-of-band OAM systems.

today: RFC 8592 is an Informational RFC published in May 2019. It provides methods for service providers to gain visibility into service function chain performance without deploying separate OAM infrastructure. The standard is used in NFV deployments where visibility into hybrid physical and virtual service chain performance is critical for operations and troubleshooting.

sections.title: Network Service Header and Performance Visibility
sections.content:
The Network Service Header (NSH), defined in RFC 8300, allows service providers to steer traffic through an ordered set of service functions—both virtual network functions (VNFs) running in software and physical network functions (PNFs) as hardware appliances. This flexibility is powerful, but it creates a visibility challenge: where does latency come from, and where is QoS configuration misconfigured?

RFC 8592 describes how to carry latency and QoS information inside NSH metadata as packets flow through the service chain. Instead of running separate out-of-band monitoring systems, these methods embed performance data directly in the packets themselves, allowing the last service function in the chain to export the complete history to a performance database for analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: When packets flow through multiple service functions in a chain, they can pick up notes about timing and quality along the way, so you can later see exactly where problems occurred.

sections.title: Stamping Architecture
sections.content:
KPI stamping involves four logical roles: The Stamping Controller (SC) decides which flows to monitor and instructs the first node. The First Stamping Node (FSN), typically a service classifier, marks NSH metadata fields to indicate how downstream service functions should behave. The service functions (SF1, SF2, etc.) apply timestamps or QoS stamps as dictated by the FSN. The Last Stamping Node (LSN) removes the NSH and exports all collected metadata to a KPI database for offline analysis and trend detection.

Each flow is identified by a combination of Service Path Identifier (SPI) and Flow ID (16 bits), allowing up to 65,536 flows to be monitored concurrently on a single service chain. The FSN inserts a Reference Time using NTP 64-bit format at the start of stamping, providing a wall-clock reference for historical comparison.
sections.plainLanguage: A controller tells the first router which flows to watch. That router marks each packet with a starting time. Each service function adds its own timing notes. The last node collects all the notes and writes them to a database for analysis.

sections.title: Two Stamping Modes: Timestamps and QoS
sections.content:
Timestamping mode captures latency by recording when packets enter and leave each service function. All service functions hosting VNFs must be synchronized to a centralized time source using NTP (Level A, millisecond accuracy) or PTP (Level B, microsecond accuracy). The method does not mandate hardware or software implementation; both are acceptable. The FSN inserts a reference time at the start, and each SF records ingress and egress timestamps if requested. The synchronization status is recorded, so out-of-sync nodes can be identified.

QoS stamping mode records Quality of Service fields at each service function to detect where QoS configuration changes or mismatches occur. It captures VLAN tags, MPLS labels, DSCP markings, and other QoS-related bits. Unlike timestamping, QoS stamping does not require time synchronization across service functions. This mode is useful for periodic audits (perhaps once per day) to verify that QoS configuration is consistent across the entire chain or parts thereof.

Both modes use three encapsulation types: Detection mode (MD Type 0x01) for simple anomaly detection using minimal header space, Timestamp Extended mode (0x02) for detailed latency analysis, and QoS Extended mode (0x03) for quality-of-service validation.
sections.plainLanguage: Timestamping records when a packet enters and exits each function, showing how much delay each one adds. QoS stamping records quality-of-service markings to spot where the packet is marked differently than expected.

sections.title: Deployment Models
sections.content:
Service providers can use KPI stamping in several deployment scenarios. Hybrid chains mix VNFs and PNFs, where only the VNFs stamp timestamps (PNFs may lack software support), but the captured Service Index helps identify where PNFs occur in the chain. Targeted VNF stamping monitors a specific service function in the middle of the chain rather than the entire chain, reducing overhead.

The Stamping Control Plane (SCP) interface between the Stamping Controller and the First Stamping Node is left for further study. This interface must support querying which flows are active, specifying which flows and chains to stamp, indicating whether to stamp ingress, egress, or both, and setting duration limits (by packet count or time).

Service providers typically apply timestamping to a large set of packets for trend analysis, but QoS stamping is applied periodically (perhaps once per day) to check configuration after a network change. If performance becomes an issue, the LSN can selectively export only a subset of KPI stamps using sampling methods.
sections.plainLanguage: You can monitor one function in the middle of the chain or the whole chain. Timestamping usually watches many packets for trends, while QoS checks are quick audits done once a day.

sections.title: Packet Format and Metadata
sections.content:
KPI metadata is carried in NSH Metadata Type 2 TLVs using the experimental Metadata Class range (0xfff6 to 0xfffe). The KPI Encapsulation Configuration Header contains an I bit (Ingress) and E bit (Egress) to indicate which timestamps are present, a T bit indicating whether Reference Time is included, a Stamping SI field specifying which service index to monitor, and a Flow ID (16 bits).

Timestamps are carried in 64-bit NTP format. Each stamping node also records a synchronization status (in-synch, in holdover, in free run, or out of synch) using a 2-bit SYN field. If a node is out of synch, it does not apply timestamps and forwards the packet unchanged.

QoS stamping captures ten standard QoS types: ingress and egress VLAN priority and drop eligibility, ingress and egress QinQ, ingress and egress MPLS experimental fields, and ingress and egress DSCP. For stacked headers, multiple QoS values are extracted into single fields for efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: The header includes flags for which timestamps are present, a reference time, a flow ID to identify which conversation is being watched, and synchronization status so you know if the timestamps are accurate.

sections.title: Performance and Implementation
sections.content:
The document does not mandate a specific stamping implementation. Hardware-based stamping incurs minimal overhead, while software stamping may add a small delay relative to normal traffic. However, these delays are assumed to be consistent for the flow being monitored, making relative timestamps meaningful even if absolute accuracy is limited.

Because KPI stamping is expected to operate on only a small percentage of user flows, performance impact is minimal in normal operation. Fragmentation of NSH metadata is supported, allowing KPI stamps to extend beyond the standard 256-octet path without requiring jumbo frames. The methods are extensible for monitoring additional KPIs beyond latency and QoS.
sections.plainLanguage: Stamping only watches a few percent of packets, so it does not slow down the network much. Timestamps are relative, so even software-based stamping can spot which function is slow.
